france24fr.title: Halloween et manifestations : interdit de dissimuler son visage ?
france24fr.description: Le message a provoqué un tollé. Mercredi, la préfecture de police rappelle que dissimuler son visage dans l'espace public est passible d'une amende, même pendant Halloween. france24fr.description: C’est officiel depuis cette nuit : la Confédération africaine de football (CAF) fait machine arrière et maintient la Coupe d'Afrique des nations (CAN) tous les deux ans. La compétition continentale continuera donc de se jouer tous les deux ans, et non tous les quatre ans. Une décision prise à l’unanimité par le comité exécutif. Une décision politique ? france24fr.title: Dans les Yvelines, des rassemblements distincts en hommage aux victimes de l'attentat raciste
france24fr.description: Deux rassemblements distincts ont eu lieu vendredi, à Trappes et à La Verrière, pour rendre hommage aux victimes de l'attentat raciste perpétré la semaine dernière dans ces deux communes des Yvelines. Des milliers de personnes se sont réunies à Trappes, où le maire Ali Rabeh a accusé les dirigeants du Rassemblement national d'avoir une responsabilité directe dans le passage à l'acte de l'assaillant.

france24fr.title: À Détroit, les votes des abstentionnistes seront déterminants
france24fr.description: Les ÉtatsUnis affichent l'un des taux d'abstention les plus élevés parmi les pays développés. Lors des élections de mi-mandat débutant mardi 3 novembre, qui mobilisent traditionnellement moins d'électeurs, ce taux dépasse régulièrement les 50 %. Convaincre les électeurs de se rendre aux urnes constitue un enjeu majeur pour les partis. Notre journaliste Valentin Cacheux s’est rendu à Détroit, où il a suivi des militants démocrates dans l'ouest de la ville.

france24fr.title: “Netanyahu n’a pas gagné, il a perdu, et de loin”, dit l’ex-Premier ministre israélien Ehud Barak
france24fr.description: Dans un entretien à France 24, l’ancien Premier ministre israélien Eoud Barak estime que Benjamin Netanyahu “n’a pas gagné” les élections mais qu’il “a perdu, et de loin”. Pour lui, son rival Gadi Eisenkot devrait s’allier aux partis arabes. Il laisse entendre que les accusations de financement qatari d’un parti arabe visent à détourner l’attention du Qatargate, et juge Netanyahu prêt à frapper l’Iran pour rester au pouvoir.

france24fr.title: L’Europe scrute les midterms américaines : si Trump perd, l’UE gagne ?
france24fr.description: L'Union européenne retient son souffle avant le résultat des midterms, les élections de mi-mandat aux États-Unis qui renouvellent le Congrès. Une majorité de dirigeants européens espère une défaite de Donald Trump lors de ce scrutin et un affaiblissement de sa politique qui veut remettre en cause le droit international et le multilatéralisme.

france24fr.title: Législatives en Israël : Netanyahu à quitte ou double ?
france24fr.description: Pour la première fois depuis les attentats du 7 octobre 2023, les électeurs israéliens ont renouvelé leur parlement. Un vote sans issue certaine concernant l'avenir politique du Premier ministre, Benjamin Netanyahu, dont la coalition perd du terrain, mais sans permettre à l'opposition de gouverner en dehors d'un accord avec les partis arabes israéliens, véritable surprise du scrutin.

france24fr.title: États-Unis : des profits financiers sans précédent pour Donald Trump
france24fr.description: Les États Unis se préparent à voter les midterms mardi 3 novembre, pour renouveler le Congrès, alors que les démocrates tentent de faire de la corruption en enjeu de ce scrutin. Les historiens affirment qu’aucun autre occupant de la Maison-Blanche n’a accumulé autant de profits financiers ou de situation de conflits d’intérêts.

france24fr.title: Guerre en Ukraine : la ville d'Olechky isolée, en proie à une crise humanitaire

spiegel.title: Ebola: Mehr als 5000 Tote in Demokratischer Republik Kongo
spiegel.description: Bei einem der schwersten Ebolaausbrüche bisher sind in der Demokratischen Republik Kongo inzwischen mehr als 5000 Menschen gestorben. Auch Nigeria, Kenia und Uganda sind betroffen.

spiegel.title: Nach rassistischem Anschlag in Frankreich: Tausende gedenken den Opfern
spiegel.description: Ein Mann schoss in Gemeinden nahe Paris mit einer automatischen Waffe gezielt auf Muslime und Menschen afrikanischer Herkunft. Während Terrorermittlungen laufen, kamen Tausende zu Soli-Kundgebungen zusammen.

spiegel.title: Nelly soll für Auftritt bei Taylor-Swift-Tour 50.000 Dollar bekommen haben
spiegel.description: »Eines Abends rief mich diese Frau völlig unerwartet an«: In einer Radiosendung plaudert Rapper Nelly darüber, wie es einst zu einem Gastauftritt auf der Tour von Popsuperstar Taylor Swift kam.

spiegel.title: Polen: Polizeieinsatz bei eskalierendem Streit über das Verfassungsgericht
spiegel.description: Polizisten vor dem Gebäude, eine abgebrochene Reise zu einem Staatsbesuch und widersprüchliche Mitteilungen aus dem Gericht: In Warschau spitzt sich ein Machtkampf über das Verfassungsgericht zu.

spiegel.title: Ukraine-Krieg: USA genehmigen Verkauf von 500 Patriot-Abwehrraketen
spiegel.description: Das US-Außenministerium hat den Verkauf von 500 Patriot-Raketen an die Ukraine freigegeben. Zuvor hatte es Streit zwischen US-Präsident Trump und dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Selenskyj über verzögerte Lieferungen gegeben.

spiegel.title: Mexiko: Rekord-Skelettfrau »Catrina« wacht über Mexiko-Stadt
spiegel.description: Hierzulande wird am Wochenende Allerheiligen begangen, in Mexiko zelebriert man den »Tag der Toten«. In der Hauptstadt gibt es noch einen weiteren Grund zu feiern.

spiegel.title: Demokratie in der Krise: Wie Bürger zum politischen Desaster beitragen - Kolumne
spiegel.description: Wir zeigen gern auf die Schuld von Politikern. Doch was ist eigentlich der Anteil der normalen Bürgerinnen und Bürger am Desaster unserer Zeit?

spiegel.title: Abdul El-Sayed: Kann er für die Demokraten die Mehrheit im Senat erobern?
spiegel.description: Donald Trump nennt ihn »Mohammed« und diffamiert ihn als »Dschihadisten«. Trotzdem liegt Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan vorn. Bei den Midterms könnte er die Mehrheit für die Demokraten erobern.

spiegel.title: EU-Kanada-Gipfel: Streit um einen Namen – »Mitgliedschaft« wird zum Störfaktor
spiegel.description: Die EU und Kanada wollen ihre Partnerschaft vertiefen. Aber wie soll die neue Verbindung heißen? Da sind sich die Beteiligten uneins – auch wenn es inhaltlich Konsens gibt.

spiegel.title: Eingewandert, um zu bleiben: Insekten auf dem Vormarsch - SPIEGEL TV
spiegel.description: Die Asiatische Hornisse oder die Große Drüsenameise: Invasive Arten breiten sich aus und gefährden die Infrastruktur. Auch die Bettwanze wird wieder zur Plage. Über den verzweifelten Kampf gegen die Krabbeltiere.

spiegel.title: Fall Fabian: Am Ende des Prozesses holt Gina H. zum Rundumschlag aus
spiegel.description: Die 30-jährige Gina H. soll den Sohn ihres Partners erstochen haben. Die Staatsanwaltschaft hält die Beweise für erdrückend, doch die Verteidigung plädiert auf Freispruch. Und die Angeklagte? Teilt aus.

spiegel.title: Frank-Walter Steinmeier in China: Bisschen wandern, Tischtennis spielen, E-Auto fahren
spiegel.description: Vier Tage China: Der scheidende Bundespräsident Frank-Walter Steinmeier reist zum Staatsbesuch in die Volksrepublik. Stets an Steinmeiers Seite: der Handelskonflikt mit der Großmacht.

spiegel.title: G20-Außenminister sperren sich gegen »Familienfoto« mit Russland
spiegel.description: Es ist ein Signal an Moskau: Das sonst oft übliche »Familienfoto« der G20-Runde fiel in Atlanta aus. Außenminister Johann Wadephul wollte sich dem Bild zunächst nicht verschließen, änderte seine Meinung aber dann.

spiegel.title: Kreuzfahrtschiff: Die »Odyssey« sollte immer weiterfahren. Sie kam bis Kambodscha
spiegel.description: Für die Aussicht auf eine endlose Kreuzfahrt an Bord der »Odyssey« haben Passagiere Häuser, Autos, Unternehmen verkauft. Nun sind sie in Kambodscha gestrandet. Der Betreiber macht bei dem plötzlichen Aus keine gute Figur.

spiegel.title: Madeleine »Maddie« McCann: Polizei darf Christian B. nicht länger observieren
spiegel.description: Christian B. gilt als Verdächtiger im Fall der in Portugal verschwundenen »Maddie«. Auch heute noch gilt er als gefährlich. Aber offenbar nicht als gefährlich genug. Deswegen endet jetzt seine polizeiliche Observation.

spiegel.title: Midterms: Papst Leo XIV. hat seine Stimme abgegeben
spiegel.description: Es sei ein Recht und eine Pflicht, an demokratischen Prozessen teilzunehmen, so Leo XIV. Daher hat er jetzt offenbar bei den amerikanischen Midterm-Wahlen seine Stimme abgegeben.

spiegel.title: Glyphosat: Bayer siegt erneut vor US-Gericht
spiegel.description: Seit Jahren wird über mögliche Gesundheitsrisiken des Pflanzenschutzmittels Glyphosat gestritten. Nun hat ein Gericht erneut zugunsten von Bayer entschieden.

spiegel.title: Donald Trump: »Air Force One« sorgt mit Halloweenflug für Schrecken in Washington
spiegel.description: Anlässlich seiner Halloweenparty hat US-Präsident Donald Trump die »Air Force One« tief über das Weiße Haus fliegen lassen. Die Boeing 747 kam den Gebäuden in der Hauptstadt sehr nahe – und sorgte damit für Schrecken.

nyt.title: Obamacare Dealt Yet Another Blow as Premiums Jump Again
nyt.description: Premiums will increase an average 13 percent next year for millions of Americans, on top of an earlier steep increase. It adds to the problems facing the program, which the Trump administration has weakened.

nyt.title: Democrats and Republicans Share Dueling Health Care Messages in Final Midterms Push
nyt.description: After concentrating on the high price of gas and groceries, Democrats are using health costs to make their case about an “affordability crisis.”

nyt.title: The Justice Department’s Unusual Election-Year Activity
nyt.description: Federal prosecutors have targeted President Trump’s political opponents and sued states over election administration just before the midterms. Devlin Barrett, a reporter for The New York Times, explains how this activity is compared with the Justice Department’s usual election-year behavior.

nyt.title: Polymarket and Kalshi Face a Major Accuracy Test: The Midterms
nyt.description: Studies have shown that the betting sites can predict races correctly, but their ability to forecast U.S. midterm elections is an important proving ground.

nyt.title: Trump Will Go to Kansas and Iowa Before Election Day
nyt.description: Also, a rare rescue begins in Ukraine. Here’s the latest at the end of Friday.

nyt.title: Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack Is Just the Start of a Risky New Era
nyt.description: The largest cyber heist in history came as attackers increasingly use artificial intelligence and other advanced techniques to steal crypto and quickly launder the funds.

nyt.title: Binance Was Hacked. What Protections Exist for Crypto Customers?
nyt.description: After a $6.3 billion hack, the company said it was going to reimburse customers who had losses.

nyt.title: Binance Lost Over $6 Billion in Crypto Hack. Here’s What to Know.
nyt.description: Hackers made off with around $6 billion in digital currency in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history. Binance said it will cover the losses.

nyt.title: Curry Barker Narrates a Scene From ‘Obsession’
nyt.description: Barker, the film’s writer and director, explains how lingering shots heighten the tension and awkwardness in a party scene.

nyt.title: Judge Appoints Special Master to Determine if Trump Officials Lied in Golf Course Suit
nyt.description: Judge Ana C. Reyes said an outside investigator would help determine whether parks officials or Justice Department lawyers withheld plans for Washington’s East Potomac Park.

nyt.title: I Covered the Tiananmen Square Massacre. It Still Weighs on Me.
nyt.description: The day that changed modern China also taught me how to recognize true courage.

nyt.title: Tech Stocks See Worst Day Since June, Pressuring Broader Market
nyt.description: The Nasdaq and the S&P 500 had their worst day since June as investors worried about spending on A.I. infrastructure.

nyt.title: Patrick Stewart Was Regal, Stately and Quite Hilarious
nyt.description: The actor used his booming voice and Shakespearean pedigree in the service of absurd (and often lewd) comedy.

nyt.title: As Picard on ‘Star Trek’, Patrick Stewart Influenced Generations of Scientists
nyt.description: Stewart’s iconic “Star Trek” character inspired astronomers and astronauts in countless ways: “You were the captain of my childhood,” one astrophysicist said.

nyt.title: Alina Habba’s Husband Ignited Drama in Trump’s Circle. Now He’s Under Scrutiny.
nyt.description: Turhan Mildon, who married Alina Habba this summer, presents himself as a 29-year-old billionaire with ties to global leaders. His story has inconsistencies.

nyt.title: Prosecutors Suggest They May Seek Additional Comey Charges
nyt.description: At a hearing in federal court, prosecutors defended an unusual, 11th-hour criminal case accusing the former F.B.I. director of leaking classified information a decade ago.

nyt.title: Christa Pike Describes Pain and Isolation After Botched Execution
nyt.description: Christa Pike, who was convicted of a 1995 murder, released her first statement since the failed attempt to execute her last month.

nyt.title: Houston Grand Jury Indicts ICE Agent on Charges of Ramming Man in Chase
nyt.description: The agent is facing charges of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. The immigrant who was struck is recovering from severe leg injuries.

npr.title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
npr.description: The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange reported Thursday that approximately $6.3 billion was impacted in an apparent hack.

npr.title: Alaska's Senate race faces claims of spoiler candidate. And, Hegseth ousts Army general
npr.description: Alaska's governor ordered an investigation into claims that Dems recruited a spoiler candidate to confuse voters. And, Hegseth ousted an Army general as the U.S. prepares for potential attacks on Iran.

npr.title: Israel is in a political deadlock. What comes next?
npr.description: Israel's consequential election has ended in a deadlock, with neither side able to claim a majority, What happens now?

npr.title: What killed 500-plus penguins? How scientists solved the mystery
npr.description: The penguins that perished lived on the Danger Islands in Antarctica. The prime suspect was avian flu. Researchers were surprised by what they found.

npr.title: US and Japan agree to establish a Japanese facility for joint missile production
npr.description: The announcement Wednesday is the latest action by the allies, who have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.

npr.title: China elevates a military general to the Politburo and seeks to strengthen party discipline
npr.description: This move comes about a year before President Xi Jinping is expected to secure his fourth five-year term.

npr.title: Greetings from Baghdad, where Agatha Christie's old home presents its own mystery
npr.description: The English writer visited Iraq multiple times in the first half of the 20th century and set some of her mystery novels there. The house in Baghdad where she once lived now sits abandoned and crumbling.

npr.title: GDP report to give insight before Election Day. And, Israel's election is deadlocked
npr.description: Economists expect the GDP report to show economic growth, but say that growth is "fragile." And, after 90% of the votes in Israel have been counted, no clear winner has emerged.

npr.title: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
npr.description: Artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable. Russia and Ukraine both use AI-powered drones, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.

npr.title: Spain reckons with 2nd deadly train crash of the year ahead of national election
npr.description: Spain's second high-speed rail disaster this year, a crash in which one train struck another from behind, killing 68 people, has raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network.

phys-org.title: Are narcissists multiplying or is the social media algorithm making them bolder? The answer in five stages

phys-org.description: A University of Massachusetts Amherst-led research team has discovered that weaker rock in mountain landscapes erodes three times faster than harder rock—even on gentler slopes—and is one of the main attributes governing mountain erosion. DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) help researchers explore these large collections by attaching a short DNA sequence to each molecule, acting as a molecular barcode that allows compounds with promising properties to be identified.

phys-org.title: Survey reveals what students think about AI

phys-org.title: UTe₂ reveals two flavors of superconductivity under extreme pressure

phys-org.title: Crop diversification protects fields from extreme weather and boosts productivity
phys-org.description: Varying crop rotations and keeping the soil constantly covered with vegetation help protect crops against droughts and floods, in addition to increasing productivity. This technique was tested in Rio Grande do Sul state, Brazil, by researchers from the Center for Carbon Research in Tropical Agriculture (CCARBON) at the University of São Paulo (USP).

phys-org.title: A decade of carbon dioxide data from space gets an upgrade
phys-org.description: Every day, two NASA space instruments known as the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 and -3 (OCO-2 and OCO-3) capture more than a million observations of sunlight reflecting off Earth's surface. Using the physics of how light travels through the air, an algorithm converts these raw data into atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) concentrations.

phys-org.title: Using less politically charged language can 'lower the temperature' on DEI training

undark.title: Body Snatchers and the Murky Process of Whole-Body Donation
undark.description: Opinion | Each year, more than 20,000 people in the U.S. donate their bodies to science after death. But the programs that handle whole-body donations lack oversight, with inconsistencies in standards of consent, transparency, and accountability. The result is reminiscent of the body-snatching practices of years past.

undark.title: Book Review: The Bizarre Frontiers of Product Testing
undark.description: From rampaging bears to zero-G toilets and chicken cannons, Alex Davies, in “Kobuk the Destroyer,” chronicles the surprising and often bizarre world of test engineering, and the ingenious lengths to which product testers will go to make the world a safer place.

undark.title: After Cancer, a Complex Aftermath for Survivors
undark.description: Around 70 percent of people with cancer today will live for more than five years after their diagnosis. They’re likely to find that life after cancer is complicated — marked by health risks and chronic illnesses — and that their primary care doctors may be ill-equipped to help them navigate it.

undark.title: Could an Amazonian Highway Open a Pandora’s Box of Pathogens?
undark.description: Brazil has plans to repave a neglected 550-mile road in the South American rainforest to help connect the region and boost economic growth. But some scientists are concerned the project — which would likely increase access between humans, livestock, and wildlife — might be a biosecurity risk.

undark.title: Interview: The Nerve That Could Transform Medicine
undark.description: Kevin Tracey, a researcher and neurosurgeon whose team discovered the vagus nerve’s link to the immune system more than two decades ago, has developed an electrical implant to stimulate the nerve in an effort to help rheumatoid arthritis sufferers who currently have difficulty taking medications.

undark.title: AI and Virtual Reality Enter the Therapist’s Office
undark.description: Some experts say that deepfake technology and other AI tools could help tackle treatment-resistant conditions like anorexia and prolonged grief. But plenty of questions remain, including whether there could be damaging side effects and whether the therapy is even effective.

undark.title: On the Weather Radar: Cloudy With a Chance of Birds
undark.description: This year’s spring migration in North America unveiled real-time measures at a higher resolution than ever before. On one night, for instance, 156 million birds appeared in the skies, outpacing the forecasted total by 20 million. And researchers figured that out thanks to AI.

undark.title: In a Long-Awaited Move, FDA Enforces Trial Result Transparency
undark.description: After years of limited oversight, the FDA sent warnings to more than 2,200 clinical trial sponsors about missing results, which were supposed to be uploaded to an official public database. Experts have pushed for greater transparency.

undark.title: Book Review: An Optimistic Defense of Uncertainty in Science
undark.description: At an uncertain moment in the sciences, Stuart Firestein argues in favor of optimism in “It Could Be Otherwise,” since uncertainty leaves room for possibility, and possibility drives curiosity, imagination, and the agency to study the peculiarities of the natural world.

undark.title: The New Importance of the Scientific Seminar
undark.description: Opinion | The rise of artificial intelligence in science complicates the notion of expertise. When AI can be used to generate ideas, conduct research, and write papers, live scientific presentations — such as public talks and seminars — become more important as a way to demonstrate who is a real expert and who is not.

proj-syn.title: Mapping AI Resistance
proj-syn.description: Since a society that is reluctant to deploy a technology will not capture its gains, it is worth understanding why the AI revolution is being welcomed in some places and resisted in others. The explanation is not as simple as headline poll data and much media coverage suggest.

proj-syn.title: The World’s Perilous Ebola Complacency
proj-syn.description: The exponential trajectory of the latest Ebola outbreak is an urgent reminder that infectious diseases do not wait for ideal geopolitical alignments or balanced budgets. Global leaders must fund the Africa-led regional response today, or risk paying an immeasurably higher price in human lives and economic devastation tomorrow.

proj-syn.title: Industrial Decarbonization Is Good for Business
proj-syn.description: With major governments showing open hostility toward climate solutions or focusing on other needs, one might think that progress toward decarbonization is in jeopardy. Yet across the global industrial sector, many companies are increasing productivity, boosting revenue growth, and reducing emissions all at once.

proj-syn.title: When the AI Bubble Bursts
proj-syn.description: Speculative bubbles often leave behind valuable infrastructure while bankrupting the investors who financed them. AI could follow the same path, but the industry’s growing reliance on borrowed money raises the risk of a major financial crisis long before its world-beating applications emerge.

proj-syn.title: After Brazil and Serbia’s Elections
proj-syn.description: The recent electoral defeat of far-right forces in Brazil and Serbia offers important lessons for pro-democracy forces around the world as they confront nationalist and illiberal movements. But no single election can guarantee democracy’s resilience, and the challenges these countries’ new governments face remain formidable.

proj-syn.title: The New Geopolitics of Mining
proj-syn.description: While the US and China want their critical-mineral investments to deliver the biggest returns possible, governments in resource-rich countries must balance external pressures with internal demands. Mining firms must also win local communities’ trust, as host countries will be quick to throw them under the bus if public opinion sours.

proj-syn.title: Can Bond Vigilantes Prevent the Next Debt Crisis?
proj-syn.description: With interest rates on government debt having gone from near zero to much higher levels in recent years, rising short- and long-term bond yields have cast doubt on the sustainability of some debts and led many to wonder if a crisis might be looming. While some countries are more protected than others, none is immune.

proj-syn.title: A Wealth Tax Would Harm California
proj-syn.description: Before approving a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires who lived in the state at a certain point in time, Californians should consider what such a policy will do to future tax revenues. Since wealth is mobile, those who stand to lose the most will simply leave, taking their future income-tax payments with them.

proj-syn.title: A Future for Europe’s Youth
proj-syn.description: The current generation of young Europeans possesses freedoms, material resources, opportunities to travel, and technological capabilities beyond anything previous generations could have imagined. Their demands, however, are strikingly simple: decent schools, secure jobs, affordable homes, and the possibility of raising a family.

proj-syn.title: A Tale of Two Chinas
proj-syn.description: China’s economy is deeply unbalanced, with a battered real-estate sector, weak consumption, and stark regional disparities coexisting with dynamic tech and export sectors. But provided that political stability is maintained, China could continue to be a global powerhouse even as hundreds of millions of its citizens remain poor.

proj-syn.title: Sino–American Stability?
proj-syn.description: Delegates at the Bund Summit in Shanghai largely agreed that the US-China relationship could be entering a new, less contentious chapter, although many were more interested in what the post-Trump era will mean for Sino-American ties. But perhaps the most heartening sign for the future was the honest exchange of views.

proj-syn.title: Europe’s Winter of Discontent
proj-syn.description: Although it is true that European integration has always been forged through crisis, the continent’s postwar story was largely one of incremental responses to relatively manageable challenges. Today, the European Union is facing multiple, interrelated problems that challenge its very raison d’être.

proj-syn.title: How Students Dethroned Serbia’s Strongman
proj-syn.description: Following the ouster of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán after 16 years in power earlier this year, the world has once again witnessed the merits of “old-school” campaigning. In toppling their own country's strongman, Serbia's new student-led opposition offers important lessons for those defending democracy elsewhere.

proj-syn.title: What a US-China AI Safety Channel Needs
proj-syn.description: Addressing AI safety risks depends on close collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and the establishment of an incident-reporting channel is just a small step in this direction. But success will require that the US and Chinese governments actually understand what is happening under their own noses.

proj-syn.title: The Authoritarian Logic of Selective Privacy
proj-syn.description: Around the world, governments are increasingly deciding who gets privacy and who is denied it, a double standard that turns a fundamental democratic right into a privilege. US President Donald Trump’s administration is a prime example, shielding ICE agents from scrutiny while expanding surveillance of immigrants and protesters.

proj-syn.title: Brazil’s Chapter in the Anti-Authoritarian Playbook
proj-syn.description: Brazil’s renewed democratic confidence must now be matched by institutional and structural reforms and a willingness to build coalitions beyond the left. Recent democratic outcomes in Hungary and Serbia offer useful lessons.

proj-syn.title: Another Crash Landing for Brazil’s Economy?
proj-syn.description: Brazil’s floating exchange rate, high foreign-exchange reserves, strong commodity exports, and debt denominated predominantly in its own currency reduce its exposure to a balance-of-payments crisis. Nonetheless, continued fiscal deterioration under President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will carry high domestic costs.
